title: Drain a stock tank by siphon: sink the hose to fill it, pinch one end and carry it out while one hand holds the intake
instruction: Drain the stock tank into the tub with the hose.
context: Farm and ranch workers empty and scrub livestock water tanks regularly to keep algae down (O*NET 45-2093.00, Farmworkers, Farm, Ranch, and Aquacultural Animals; NC State Extension, Controlling Algae in Livestock Water Tanks), and a tank with no drain plug is emptied with a hose siphon. Sucking on the hose to start it means swallowing algae-laden tank water (CDC lists swallowing water as the way people get sick from harmful algae), so the hose is started by sinking it until it fills, closing one end with a thumb or a pinch, carrying that end out over the rim and down below the tank's water while the other end stays under, and only then opening it. Lifted out open, the hose drains back, and the light intake end, once the stiff hose is bent out over the rim, springs up out of the water unless a hand holds it down, so with no clip or weight on the rim one hand keeps it down until the tank is empty. The tank then runs down to the intake and the siphon stops by itself.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0. The scene is a 1:5 model (lengths), so the tank stands for a 3.3 ft round poly stock tank of about 50 gallons. Stock tank (fixed): a gray poly round tank, 20 cm across and 5.8 cm deep inside (5 mm wall and floor), standing on a concrete pad 19 x 23 x 3.7 cm (the tank overhangs it 1 cm front and back), both centered at x 33, y 0; its inside floor is 4.2 cm up and its rim 10 cm up. It holds 1,571 mL of water, 5 cm deep, surface 9.2 cm up, drawn as a green-gray column. Tub (fixed): a black rubber tub 20 cm across and 6.2 cm deep inside (floor 3 mm), centered at x 27, y -21.5, empty. Hose ends (two, loose): a pine stick 2.5 x 2.5 cm, 7.9 cm tall, on a foot plate 4 x 4 x 0.6 cm (8.5 cm overall), with a clear end tube 1.4 cm across taped to one face from 0.8 cm (the open mouth, pointing down) to 3.5 cm up, where the soft 12.7 mm bore vinyl hose joins it. The intake (green tape, plastic foot, 40 g in all) stands at x 22, y 20, its tube on its left (+y) face; its hose leaves the top of its end tube. The outlet (red tape, steel foot, 120 g) stands at x 21, y -9, turned so its tube faces the robot (-x), angled 23 degrees toward its right; its hose is taped on up that face of the stick to the top (3.9 cm front to back with the hose) and leaves over it, so fingers closed front to back across it squeeze the hose shut. The hose (60 cm, 76 mL) is drawn between the ends: pale when dry, water-colored where it holds water, and a stream from the outlet while it runs.
scoring: Definitions: the hose fills while both mouths and both end-tube tops are under the tank's surface, the outlet is open and no more than 10 mL of air is left where the outlet's taped run stands above the water (up the stick and back down: 9 mL with the outlet standing on the tank's floor, a slug the starting flow of 0.6 m/s sweeps out), in 2 s (a real 10 ft hose takes about 10 s, until the bubbles stop). The outlet is pinched shut while a gripper is closed across its stick and taped hose (the opening stopped by the 3.9 cm width), its tool point at least 5 cm up the stick and its fingers closing within 30 degrees of square across the hose; fingers on the plain faces, an empty fist or an open hand do not close it. While primed, open and with the intake's mouth at least 5 mm under the surface (shallower, it gulps air), water runs at k sqrt(head), k = 283 mL/s per sqrt(m) for a 12.7 mm bore, 60 cm hose (81 mL/s at the starting 8.1 cm head), into the vessel the outlet's mouth is in, else onto the floor (spilled). The prime is lost, and it counts for the rest of the trial, when the intake's mouth comes out of the water, when the open outlet's mouth is above the tank's surface for one control step (the hose drains back), or when the tank is drawn down to the intake (the normal end: surface 5.5 cm up, 1,162 mL above that). The intake end is light and the hose stiff: whenever the outlet's mouth is outside the tank (the hose bent out over the rim) while no gripper holds the intake (fingers stopped by its stick), the intake is up at the rim, out of the water. Scores: 0 if either end is still held at the end (any tool point or pad tip within 1 cm of it, open or closed), if more than 20 mL spilled (a quarter second of the starting stream), or if under 25 % of the 1,162 mL reached the tub (nothing done, never primed, one hand only). 0.25 if at least a quarter reached the tub but the prime was lost on the way (the outlet carried out open, the intake let go before the tank was empty or lifted out), even if it was started again. 0.5 if primed and never lost but stopped short with under 90 % (1,046 mL) in the tub (the intake held off the floor: 1 cm up leaves 27 % behind). 0.75 if drained but an end left outside its vessel (the outlet's mouth not in the tub, or the intake's not in the tank or the tub). 1.0 with both arms back home and still; 0.9 if not. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, weigh the tub and the mopped-up spill, and check from the video that the outlet crossed the rim pinched and that a hand stayed on the intake until the tank was empty; the drawn-down end is the hose gulping air.
reset_notes: Empty the hose, stand both ends on their marks, refill the tank to the 5 cm line (1,571 mL) and empty and dry the tub and the table. Run with -E object_jitter=0 (one fixed layout).
fidelity: Lengths are at 1:5 and there is no fluid: the water is a flow model (levels from volumes, flow k sqrt(head) through a 12.7 mm bore, 60 cm hose), so the tank drains in about 30 s, not the 10 to 15 minutes of a real one, and the sunk hose fills in 2 s. The hose is drawn, not simulated: an unheld intake rising while the hose is bent over the rim is a rule, the air left in the outlet's taped run is counted, and the pinch is read from the grip on the rigid stand-in for the taped hose.
